overview: This bill renews and updates the National Landslide Preparedness Act, a 2020 law under which the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), the Interior Department's science agency, maps landslide hazards, studies them and helps communities prepare. It extends the landslide program's funding authorization through 2030 at up to $35 million a year, with at least $10 million for landslide early warning systems in high-risk areas, and extends a related 3D land-elevation mapping program through 2034. It adds attention to landslides triggered by atmospheric rivers (long bands of moisture that bring heavy rain), extreme rainfall, volcanoes, earthquakes and thawing permafrost, sets up regional research partnerships, and makes tribal organizations, Native Hawaiian organizations and colleges eligible for more involvement and grants. It also creates a Next Generation Water Observing System at USGS for real-time flood and drought data and expands federal stream gauge and groundwater monitoring, paid for out of existing USGS funds. The Senate passed it, and as of January 7, 2026, it was being held at the desk in the House.
for: Supporters say landslides and floods kill people and damage property every year, and better mapping, monitoring and early warning systems can save lives and help communities plan.
against: Critics say the bill raises spending authorizations for several programs, and directing new systems to be funded from existing USGS money could squeeze the agency's other work.
